text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
Robusta futures in London ended higher but failed to keep pace with another surge in New York arabica futures amid news of a planned strike by Brazilian port workers.

However, the supply situation in the robusta sector is not as tight as in the arabica sector where large harvests from Vietnam, Cameroon, Ivory Coast and possibly Indonesia are looming in the background. March ended $57 higher at $1,642 per tonne, while May gained $55 to close at $1,652 per tonne. In New York the market missed reaching the 200 cents/lb level by a mere 50 points and settled 1.45 cents/lb shy of this target. March closed 8.05 cents/lb higher at 198.45 cents/lb, while May added 8.00 cents/lb to close at 184.85 cents/lb.

Traders said the surge to new highs was a continuation of the physical tightness with March open interest remaining high, only a minimal increase in certified coffee stocks on February 28 and shorts facing the prospect of having to cover if they cannot get the coffee. There seems to be very little coffee around and this is not expected to change until new crop supplies become available. Hence, March and May must be expected to remain extremely tight.
A possible dockworkers' strike in Brazil is another element of uncertainty, but is not the overruling factor as coffee shipments are not likely to be greatly affected.

Another positive element was a report from Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes forecasting Colombia's 1996/97 crop to fall to 20-year lows. The crop would likely come in between 9.4 and 10.5 million 60-kg bags, Ganes said. Finally, the market was aided by CFTC data showing a smaller- than-expected speculative long position. Commitment of traders numbers released over the weekend showed speculators were net long some 14,000 lots as of February 25, including non- reportable positions.

GERMANY - Coffee sales dropped by 1 billion DM to 8.1 billion DM in 1996, the German Coffee Association DKV said. This was ascribed to falling retail prices, which for roasted coffee averaged only DM 7.01 in 1996. The volume declined by 0.4 per cent. 562,250 tonnes (approximately 9.4 million 60-kg bags) of raw coffee were processed into roast and ground and solubles. Per capita consumption of raw coffee in 1996 was 6.9 kg, unchanged from the previous year. However, sales of roasted coffee fell to 443,000 tonnes, from 445,000 tonnes in 1995. The slight fall in volume in 1996 continues the negative trend witnessed since 1993. This means that consumption has declined in spite of falling retail prices. Another worry is the rise in world coffee prices. DKV said 'significant' retail price rises are inevitable to compensate roasters for rising costs. ETHIOPIA - According to industry sources coffee exports in fiscal 1996/97 could reach a record 1.8 million 60-kg bags. Actual exports are expected to be even higher, due to illegal trade. According to a Reuters report a spokeswoman for the Ethiopian Tea and Coffee Authority denied that production would be less than the annual average of 4.2 million bags. According to official sources legal exports in 1995/96 of 1.7 million bags earned $279.5 million - lower than the $300.9 million it received for exporting 1.3 million bags of coffee in 1994/95. However, export revenues in 1996/97 are forecast to be higher due to higher world market prices and higher exports. Coffee is Ethiopia's main export commodity and accounts for about 60 per cent of the country's hard currency earnings.

DENMARK - Denmark imported 83,689 bags of coffee in November 1996, 11 per cent less than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 922,100 bags, 16 per cent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 14 per cent to 873,700 bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/November 1996 were Brazil (251,300 vs 298,800 bags) and Colombia (192,100 vs 165,100 bags). The country exported 94,400 bags of coffee in January/November 1996, 12 per cent more than was exported the same period in 1995. Total exports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 5.5 per cent to 91,200 bags.
